explanation: In Japan, crossing your legs while sitting is considered rude in formal and business situations because it can read as self-important or overly casual. Proper posture — back straight, legs together, hands on knees, or seiza in traditional settings — signals humble listening and respect. The custom has deep roots in Japanese etiquette, where body positioning reflects respect for others and the situation.
local_tip: In meetings and interviews, keep both feet flat on the floor with your back straight and hands resting on your knees rather than crossing your legs.
regional_note: International companies in Japan often blend Japanese and Western norms, and awareness of generational differences matters in client meetings, so expectations can be looser in some workplaces.

also_check.note: Crossing legs is common and generally read as relaxed or confident, not disrespectful.
Formal settings favor upright, respectful posture; crossing legs can seem casual, especially with elders.
Showing the sole of your shoe or crossing legs toward others is offensive in formal and social settings.
